subcomponents.title: Uses stable identities and appropriate grouped-scene architecture

criteria.rationale: Grouping: steps/index.ts maps all nine NARRATION entries to one Step shape with the same Scene (SampleScene) and groupKey 'scene'. Stage keys its motion.div with sceneKey(step), and steps.ts builds that key as `group:scene#<sceneId>` from the groupKey and the Scene identity, so it is identical for all nine steps. The one mounted Scene instance therefore only receives a new payload { step: i+1 }, with no remount. Identity: the presentation-owned ENTITIES in entities.ts carry stable ids. Scene.tsx filters them by appearsAt <= payload.step and renders each with key={e.id} and id={e.id}. Box, Label, SymbolChip, Emphasis and Frame pass props through NodeShell, which sets layoutId={id}, and Arrow sets layoutId={id} directly. Stage wraps the scene in LayoutGroup. Persisting entities therefore morph in place across steps, and newcomers get enter. The groupKey preserves the Scene mount, and the separate layoutId values preserve entity identity. All nine steps share one steps/index.ts and one narration.ts, so no per-step module is skipped.

subcomponents.title: Verification tooling robustness

criteria.rationale: startPreview launches Vite's own bin directly with node, so there is no npm or npx wrapper. It runs as a detached process group, and stop() sends SIGTERM to the whole group (-pid), awaits the child's 'exit' promise, then escalates to SIGKILL and awaits again. When readiness times out, startPreview calls stop() itself before throwing. In verify.mjs and inspect-presentation.mjs, both the repository copies and the bootstrap template copies, main() assigns `preview` inside try and runs `await browser?.close().catch(()=>{}); await preview?.stop()` in finally. Every path the guidance names goes through that finally: success (return 0), a failing check or later error (catch, return 1), and a chromium.launch() failure (thrown after preview is set). The bootstrap preview.mjs is the same code (detached, process.kill(-pid), awaited exit). E2E-001/E2E-002 check that no preview is still listening after a passing run and after render faults. I am ruling with judges A and B. Judge C fails it because the SIGINT/SIGTERM handlers call process.exit(130) and skip the finally block. The code does show that, but signal-driven termination is not one of the exit paths the guidance names (success, a failing check, a browser launch failure, an error after the preview started), and the rules forbid failing on an unnamed scenario. So C's reason does not decide this requirement.

criteria.rationale: There are three delivered tests that drive a real browser, all of them by spawning a script: tests/e2e/verify.test.ts, tests/integration/inspect.test.ts and tests/integration/bootstrap.test.ts (which runs `npm run verify`). None of them sleeps for a fixed time. Every browser run goes through sandbox `run()`, which resolves only on the child's 'close' event (sandbox.ts:14-23). Each assertion then reads the exit code, the output or the manifest written by a process that has already finished. None of these tests calls waitForTimeout, setTimeout as a delay, or a sleep. The only `setTimeout` in verify.test.ts (line 116) is text inside an injected fault string that gets written into the sample. The only `waitForTimeout` in tests/ is a no-op `async () => {}` on the mocked page in the unit test (verify-script.test.ts:110), so it does not wait for anything. In that mock, step advancement goes through a waitForFunction stub that checks the index (lines 116-118). Where the scripts move between steps, they first wait on observable state: `waitForFunction` polls data-step-index with a timeout (verify.mjs:110-117, inspect-presentation.mjs:257) before reading or capturing. Panels A and B are borne out. Panel C cites settle(): `page.waitForTimeout(SETTLE_MS)` (verify.mjs:90/119) and inspect's `waitForTimeout(opts.settleMs)` (inspect-presentation.mjs:260). Those are in the delivered verify and inspect tools, not in the tests. They run only after the state wait on data-step-index has confirmed the step, so they do not replace waiting for state. The test's own `--settle 1700` (inspect.test.ts:15,26) sets a capture-settle option that the test checks as a product behaviour (lines 75-79). It is not a sleep the test uses before asserting a step. So Panel C's reason does not show a browser test sleeping instead of waiting for state.

votes.rationale: Grouping: steps/index.ts maps all nine NARRATION entries to one Step shape with the same Scene (SampleScene) and groupKey 'scene'. Stage keys its motion.div with sceneKey(step), and steps.ts builds that key as `group:scene#<sceneId>` from the groupKey and the Scene identity, so it is identical for all nine steps. The one mounted Scene instance therefore only receives a new payload { step: i+1 }, with no remount. Identity: the presentation-owned ENTITIES in entities.ts carry stable ids. Scene.tsx filters them by appearsAt <= payload.step and renders each with key={e.id} and id={e.id}. Box, Label, SymbolChip, Emphasis and Frame pass props through NodeShell, which sets layoutId={id}, and Arrow sets layoutId={id} directly. Stage wraps the scene in LayoutGroup. Persisting entities therefore morph in place across steps, and newcomers get enter. The groupKey preserves the Scene mount, and the separate layoutId values preserve entity identity. All nine steps share one steps/index.ts and one narration.ts, so no per-step module is skipped.

votes.rationale: The verifier reserves an ephemeral port with freePort and starts the preview with --strictPort. But freePort closes the socket before the child binds. Readiness then comes only from HTTP polling: `probe(`${origin}/`)`, with a check of the `exited` flag at the top of each loop iteration. The child's own announcement of its address is never read. Readiness polling is not raced against the child's exit. Another process that grabbed the port in that gap would answer the probe before the child's exit was observed. This is the liveness-sampled-before-each-request pattern that the guidance says does not establish ownership.
evidence: startPreview: loop `if (exited) throw ...; if (await probe(`${origin}/`)) return ...; await sleep(150)`
freePort closes the server before the child is spawned
The child's stdout is only buffered for error messages and is never parsed for a readiness announcement
No Promise.race between readiness and the child's exit

A missing or non-numeric hook cannot satisfy it. On timeout it throws `transition failed` with step i. The count is read as Number(attribute). A null attribute becomes 0 and fails `count < 1`. The tests then assert on the exit code, the output or the manifest, so nothing is read before the process has finished. - **The scripts wait on state first.** Before each step, both scripts poll `data-step-index` with `page.waitForFunction`, which has a timeout. For the first step, they wait for `data-step-count` with `waitForSelector`. - **The fixed delays come after that state wait.** `settle()` in `scripts/verify.mjs` and `waitForTimeout(opts.settleMs)` in `scripts/inspect-presentation.mjs` run only once the step index is confirmed. They add a delay on top of the state check; they do not replace it. - **The inspect settle is a tested feature.** The `--settle` value is a capture option, and `inspect.test.ts` checks it as product behaviour (`capturedAt - navigatedAt >= SETTLE`). demo-integration.rationale: Talk.tsx only passes title, steps, className and initialMode to the kit's Presentation. It has no navigation, chrome or stage logic of its own. The shared Scene builds every entity from kit primitives (Box, Label, Arrow, SymbolChip, Emphasis, Frame inside SceneLayer) and forwards id and enter. Those ids reach NodeShell and Arrow, which supply the layoutId morph and the enter behaviour. steps/index.ts uses the kit's Step type with a shared Scene and a groupKey. Presentation wires the kit's nav hook, Header, Stage, Footer and Attribution. The demo does not bypass or duplicate any kit mechanism.

demo-integration.rationale: Grouping: all nine steps come from one map in steps/index.ts, so they share SampleScene and groupKey 'scene'. The step-module chain is index.ts, narration.ts and Scene.tsx, and every step is covered by it. sceneKey in steps.ts yields the same `group:scene#<id>` for all of them. Stage keys its motion.div by that value, so one Scene instance stays mounted and only the payload changes. This matches the canonical single-groupKey design. scene-kit.rationale: The source supports the pass. Layout motion uses LAYOUT_TRANSITION = {duration: LAYOUT_T (0.6), ease} with no delay. It is applied through transition={{ layout: ... }} on NodeShell and on Arrow's motion.svg. A newcomer (enter=true) gets enterProps → initial {opacity:0} and animate {opacity:1, transition:{duration 0.4, delay ENTER_DELAY 0.65}}. 0.65 is at least 0.6, so the visible entry starts after the continuing layout morph ends. The delay sits only in the opacity animate transition, so it does not delay the continuing entities' layout motion. A continuing entity gets only animate {opacity:1}, with no initial value and no delay. In the sample, Scene.tsx's Node switch renders all six entity kinds (box, label, arrow, chip, emphasis, frame) and passes enter to each. first_results.rationale: renderRoute presses ArrowRight for every step after the first. It then waits for data-step-index to equal String(i) using strict string equality (scripts/verify.mjs:107-117). If the hook is absent, the comparison sees undefined; if it is non-numeric, the strings differ. Neither can satisfy the check. On timeout the verifier throws a render PhaseError carrying step i. main prints `FAIL verify [render] (step N)` and returns 1 (verify.mjs:173-180). The step count is read with Number(...) and rejected unless it is an integer of at least 1 (verify.mjs:103-104). A null count becomes 0 and NaN fails Number.isInteger, so an unreadable count cannot step through zero steps and still pass. A missing count hook times out and fails at step 0 (99-102). The e2e 'stalled-transition' case caps navigation at index 3 and asserts a non-zero exit with `FAIL verify [render] (step 5).*transition failed` (tests/e2e/verify.test.ts:121-144). The unit test 'fails a stalled transition, naming the step' asserts {phase:'render', step:3}. Judge B's reason is that the initial index is never validated. That does not decide the criterion. The guidance's fail condition is a transition check that converts an absent or non-numeric hook into a number that still passes its comparison. Here there is no comparison at i=0 that accepts Number(null). The numeric index from readStep is never compared (compareStep checks only era, title and caption, lines 59-67). And for the nine-step sample, a missing or bad index fails at the first transition's string comparison. So no missing or non-numeric hook is treated as progress.

audit_results.rationale: The quoted lines meet every part of the criterion. On each transition the verifier presses ArrowRight. It then requires data-step-index to strictly equal String(i), so an absent hook (undefined) or a non-numeric value cannot pass. No number conversion happens at that comparison. The step count goes through Number(), but anything that is not an integer of at least 1 is rejected. That covers null becoming 0, an empty string becoming 0, and non-numeric values becoming NaN, so an unreadable count cannot step through zero steps and still pass. A missing count hook fails at step 0. A failed transition throws a render PhaseError carrying the step. main prints 'FAIL verify [render] (step N)' and returns 1. The required test exists: the e2e 'stalled-transition' case breaks advancement and asserts a non-zero exit code and stderr matching '[render] (step 5).*transition failed', which names the offending step. A unit test also asserts {phase:'render', step:3}. Index 0 is never checked, but that is not treated as progress: no transition is compared there, so the guidance's fail conditions do not apply.

audit_results.rationale: The fixture requires that the helper not report overlap warnings for elements inside a subtree marked as allowing overlap. findOverlaps skips a pair only when both elements are marked (`if (p.allow && q.allow) continue`). An element inside the marked subtree that intersects an unmarked element is therefore still reported. The candidate's own unit test proves this: it asserts the warning 'item0 overlaps item1', where item0 is marked allow:true. That is an overlap warning for an element inside the marked subtree, so this clause of the requirement is unmet. The guidance says skipping every pair with at least one marked element is a correct reading, which matches the fixture's plain meaning that marked elements are exempt. This helper reports exactly those pairs instead. A test showing that two marked elements are exempt does not cure that.

first_results.rationale: startPreview launches Vite's own bin directly with node, so there is no npm or npx wrapper. It runs as a detached process group, and stop() sends SIGTERM to the whole group (-pid), awaits the child's 'exit' promise, then escalates to SIGKILL and awaits again. When readiness times out, startPreview calls stop() itself before throwing. In verify.mjs and inspect-presentation.mjs, both the repository copies and the bootstrap template copies, main() assigns `preview` inside try and runs `await browser?.close().catch(()=>{}); await preview?.stop()` in finally. Every path the guidance names goes through that finally: success (return 0), a failing check or later error (catch, return 1), and a chromium.launch() failure (thrown after preview is set). The bootstrap preview.mjs is the same code (detached, process.kill(-pid), awaited exit). E2E-001/E2E-002 check that no preview is still listening after a passing run and after render faults. I am ruling with judges A and B. Judge C fails it because the SIGINT/SIGTERM handlers call process.exit(130) and skip the finally block. The code does show that, but signal-driven termination is not one of the exit paths the guidance names (success, a failing check, a browser launch failure, an error after the preview started), and the rules forbid failing on an unnamed scenario. So C's reason does not decide this requirement.

first_results.rationale: None of the delivered browser-driving tests sleeps for a fixed time. tests/e2e/verify.test.ts and tests/integration/inspect.test.ts drive the browser by running the project scripts through sandbox.run(), which resolves only on the child's 'close' event. They assert on exit code, stdout/stderr, manifest.json and screenshot pixels only after that has resolved, so they wait on observable state. Inside the scripts, each step advance waits on data-step-index with page.waitForFunction (a polling wait with a timeout) before anything is read. The only waitForTimeout in tests/ is a no-op stub in the mocked page of verify-script.test.ts, and the only setTimeout is inside a string injected as a page-error fault. I am ruling with judges A and B. Judge C fails it on the scripts' settle delays (inspect's --settle waitForTimeout and verify's settle()). Those delays belong to the product under test, not to the tests. INT-002 deliberately tests that inspect waits its settle interval (capturedAt - navigatedAt >= SETTLE). Both scripts wait for the step-index state before settling. The guidance also calls fixed settle delays validator noise. So C's reason does not show a test waiting a fixed time instead of waiting for state.

results.rationale: There are three delivered tests that drive a real browser, all of them by spawning a script: tests/e2e/verify.test.ts, tests/integration/inspect.test.ts and tests/integration/bootstrap.test.ts (which runs `npm run verify`). None of them sleeps for a fixed time. Every browser run goes through sandbox `run()`, which resolves only on the child's 'close' event (sandbox.ts:14-23). Each assertion then reads the exit code, the output or the manifest written by a process that has already finished. None of these tests calls waitForTimeout, setTimeout as a delay, or a sleep. The only `setTimeout` in verify.test.ts (line 116) is text inside an injected fault string that gets written into the sample. The only `waitForTimeout` in tests/ is a no-op `async () => {}` on the mocked page in the unit test (verify-script.test.ts:110), so it does not wait for anything. In that mock, step advancement goes through a waitForFunction stub that checks the index (lines 116-118). Where the scripts move between steps, they first wait on observable state: `waitForFunction` polls data-step-index with a timeout (verify.mjs:110-117, inspect-presentation.mjs:257) before reading or capturing. Panels A and B are borne out. Panel C cites settle(): `page.waitForTimeout(SETTLE_MS)` (verify.mjs:90/119) and inspect's `waitForTimeout(opts.settleMs)` (inspect-presentation.mjs:260). Those are in the delivered verify and inspect tools, not in the tests. They run only after the state wait on data-step-index has confirmed the step, so they do not replace waiting for state. The test's own `--settle 1700` (inspect.test.ts:15,26) sets a capture-settle option that the test checks as a product behaviour (lines 75-79). It is not a sleep the test uses before asserting a step. So Panel C's reason does not show a browser test sleeping instead of waiting for state.

The child is detached, so stop() can SIGTERM the whole process group via -child.pid. In the repository and bootstrap template copies of verify.mjs and inspect-presentation.mjs, `preview` is assigned inside try and `await browser?.close()...; await preview?.stop()` runs in finally. The repository and template preview.mjs are identical. The E2E tests confirm no preview is still listening after a passing run and after render faults. Signal-driven exit through the process.exit(130) handlers is not one of the exit paths the guidance names, so it cannot make a fail. Caveat: the scripts' import lines are not quoted; startPreview is taken to be the lib function because its return shape ({origin, stop}) matches.

audit_results.rationale: The criterion asks that the delivered browser-driving tests wait for observable state before they assert, and that they use no fixed sleeps. The quoted tests meet both conditions. The e2e verify test, the inspect integration test and the bootstrap integration test drive the browser by spawning the verify and inspect scripts through sandbox run(). run() resolves only when the child process emits 'close', so every assertion reads the exit code, output or manifest of a process that has already finished. That is a wait on observable state, not on a fixed delay. None of the quoted test code calls waitForTimeout, a sleep, or a setTimeout used as a delay. The setTimeout at verify.test.ts:116 is text inside an injected fault string that is written into the sample. The waitForTimeout at verify-script.test.ts:110 is a no-op stub on a mock page, and step advancement in that mock goes through a waitForFunction stub that checks the step index. The scripts the tests launch also move between steps by polling data-step-index with waitForFunction and a timeout (verify.mjs:110-117, inspect-presentation.mjs:257). Their settle delays come after that state wait, so they do not replace it. In inspect, the settle interval is a capture option the test checks as product behaviour (inspect.test.ts:75-79), not a sleep the test uses before asserting a step. Nothing quoted shows a browser test sleeping for a fixed time instead of waiting for state, or treating an immediate read as if it had waited.

result.rationale: startPreview launches Vite's own bin directly with node, so there is no npm or npx wrapper. It runs as a detached process group, and stop() sends SIGTERM to the whole group (-pid), awaits the child's 'exit' promise, then escalates to SIGKILL and awaits again. When readiness times out, startPreview calls stop() itself before throwing. In verify.mjs and inspect-presentation.mjs, both the repository copies and the bootstrap template copies, main() assigns `preview` inside try and runs `await browser?.close().catch(()=>{}); await preview?.stop()` in finally. Every path the guidance names goes through that finally: success (return 0), a failing check or later error (catch, return 1), and a chromium.launch() failure (thrown after preview is set). The bootstrap preview.mjs is the same code (detached, process.kill(-pid), awaited exit). E2E-001/E2E-002 check that no preview is still listening after a passing run and after render faults. I am ruling with judges A and B. Judge C fails it because the SIGINT/SIGTERM handlers call process.exit(130) and skip the finally block. The code does show that, but signal-driven termination is not one of the exit paths the guidance names (success, a failing check, a browser launch failure, an error after the preview started), and the rules forbid failing on an unnamed scenario. So C's reason does not decide this requirement.

engineering-quality.rationale: The auditor says all three clauses are met, but the second clause fails. That clause requires the template scripts to reject an unregistered slug with a clear non-zero failure "rather than timing out". The template inspect script never checks the slug against the registry. It opens the route and waits up to 8000 ms for `[data-step-count]`. Only when that wait expires does it throw PhaseError, and even then the message only asks "(is the slug registered?)". So the rejection depends on the timeout, which is exactly the behaviour the requirement rules out. The auditor admits the detection mechanism is the 8 s selector wait. Wrapping that timeout in a readable message and exiting 1 does not change the fact that the slug is caught by timing out, not by a registry check. The other points (verify loops over every registry entry, the slug comes from an argument, there are no reference-sample strings) do not fix this clause, so the fail verdict stands.

engineering-quality.rationale: The contradiction does not hold. The criterion asks that every readiness wait has a timeout, and the readiness wait in both preview.mjs copies has one: a 30s default deadline loop. When the loop runs out, it stops the preview and throws a PhaseError. The auditor's point is that one fetch() inside probe() has no abort signal. That defeats the verdict only if a probe to the local vite preview stalls with no response, and the material never shows that happening. The review guidance does not name that scenario, and the judging rules say not to fail a criterion on a hypothetical input the guidance does not name. Node's built-in fetch also has its own connect and header timeouts (Node behaviour, not shown in the material), so even a stalled probe would not hang forever. The auditor also agrees that the build-before-preview clause is met (verify awaits runBuild before startPreview) and that the ready-URL parsing clause does not apply, since readiness probes over HTTP instead of parsing printed output. So all three clauses are met and the pass stands.

scripts/verify.mjs and the template copy: main awaits `runBuild(root)` before `startPreview(root)`. inspect-presentation.mjs awaits runBuild when it builds, and otherwise uses an existing dist.
Readiness is detected by an HTTP probe, not by parsing printed output, so the ANSI and chunk-split parsing clause does not apply.
